translations.text: Beloved, it is clear to everyone that no one has written the books except by the grace of the Holy Spirit.
For the great Moses first began to describe heaven and earth, which he had never seen; but through the revelation of the Holy Spirit he described them as if he had seen them with his eyes.
And after him others also wrote books, in which they told the story of the children of Israel in order, one thing after another, up to his death.
Then were written down the sayings that they preached about the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ and about his struggle in the flesh.
And after the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ these four were written,
through which the coming of the Lord is proclaimed to the generations to come, along with his dispensation in the flesh that he took from the Virgin Mary out of mercy for us,
and, after this, how they went about the whole world and preached the word of life,
and many believed them and "were baptized in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit."
But the enemy and envier never ceased from opposing the truth. He stirred up the kings of that time, and they forced the believers to serve their idols,
and those of them who did not obey, they slew with the edge of the sword and burned with fire.
Then some men among the believers arose and began to write the lives of the holy martyrs and the manner in which their struggle came to its end,
for the glorification of the holy martyrs and as an example for those who have divine zeal to imitate.
For this same reason I too, though unworthy, wished to imitate those who came before, and I have written the life and martyrdom of the holy and blessed martyr Constantine,
who lived in our own days, in the reign of the God-fearing Empress Theodora, who ruled the kingdom of the Greeks while her son Michael was still a child.
This blessed woman purified all the land of the Greeks from the error that had existed in the days of her husband, the unbelief concerning icons.
She strengthened the struggle of the Greeks and rebuilt many towns that had been laid waste by the Hagarenes.
At that time there was a man in the land of Kartli, in the districts of Zena Sopeli, whose name was Constantine. He was called Kakhay after the name of his native land.
This man was very greatly distinguished throughout the land of Kartli. He had great wealth and many of the pleasures of this world.
His name was famous in distant lands, so much so that even kings had heard of him.
And this blessed man was adorned with both kinds of deeds, as a tree is adorned with leaves and fruit.
He had faith in our Lord Jesus Christ that did not waver and was firmer than the mountains.
The blessed man also had faith in the bishops and in all the clergy of the church, as is fitting and right.
He loved monks and had faith in them, and he was eager to serve them. And if any of the monks,
or any of the clergy at all, came to his house, he would go out to meet him with joy, bow down before him with his face to the ground, give him ample rest, and send him on his way with many gifts.
As for his hospitality to strangers and his mercy to the poor, no one is able to tell of them worthily; we will say only a little.
Who ever came to him, and where, hungry or thirsty, and he did not feed him until he was full? Or naked, and he did not gladly clothe him?
Many fled to him from distant lands, running from their creditors, and he paid off their debts with great gladness.
Where did he ever see an orphan or a widow and not quickly take care of them?
And besides all this, he took great care of the needy of his own household, for he had heard what the apostle Paul said:
"If anyone does not provide for his own, and especially for those of his household, he has denied the faith and is worse than the unbelievers."
The blessed man had more humility and self-abasement than anyone else, for he had heard the word of the Deliverer and Savior:
"Learn from me, for I am meek and lowly." He counted himself more sinful than anyone else and wept for his sins, and he often said:
"I have no hope of the forgiveness of sins from anywhere, except by shedding my blood for him who shed his blood for us."
His heart longed to go to the temple in Jerusalem and to worship at holy Golgotha, where our renewal was accomplished by the right hand of the Most High,
and at the life-giving Tomb clothed in light, and at holy Zion, mother of the churches, and at all the holy places where the feet of the Lord had stood.
When he reached Jerusalem, he venerated the holy places and gave great wealth to the churches,
to the poor and to the inhabitants of Jerusalem. Then he left Jerusalem and went round all the monasteries of the desert and the people living by the Jordan.
Through him they were granted much relief and comfort, and they sent him on his way with many prayers and blessings.
When he returned to his own land, he lived a splendid life, with much service to God.
From then on he never stopped asking eagerly about the peace of Jerusalem and the support of the poor
who lived there. Every year he sent three myriads (thirty thousand) of silver by one of his servants:
some of it for the holy places, some for the desert monasteries, and some for the poor who lived in Jerusalem.
For he had heard the commandment that the apostle Paul wrote to the Corinthians:
"Let your surplus go to the needs of those who are in Jerusalem, so that their surplus may also go to your need."
He grew old, and the blessed man reached the age of eighty-five.
At just this time of his life a great persecution arose against the Christians throughout the whole land of Kartli.
There were great battles, and many Christians who were fighting for the law of Christ were killed in them.
The blessed man was taken captive, since he was the leader and the most eminent man in all the land of Kartli and the head of his family.
They put him in fetters, took him in that state to the city of Tiflis, and locked him in prison.
But he was not afraid at all, nor was he shaken. Instead he accepted with joy what had come upon him, and he gave thanks to the Lord.
The seizure of that blessed man did not happen without God,
but through Him who governs all things and gives the human race occasions for salvation by His hidden providence.
In this too He willed that joyful peace [?], so that the good leaven of his zeal, which He had known beforehand, might be a spectacle for angels and men.
So He did not hold back his being seized beforehand [?], for He trusted in his courage, just as it was with Job and with all the saints, one after another.
When they brought the blessed man before the tyrant in Tbilisi, whose name was Bugha, the tyrant reproached him and said to him:
"Did you not know that you would escape from my hands by your flight? For there is no one among the rebels whom I have not overcome,
nor anyone who prepares to fight against us whom we do not overpower. For behold, God has given you to us this day, to be slaughtered by our hands!"
The blessed Constantine answered him and said: "I too know that God has given us into your hands, but not because He loves you,
nor because of your good deeds. It is because we did not keep His commandments, and for this reason He has cut us down by means of that nation of disobedience.
For many times the Lord also gave Israel into the hands of foreigners, whenever they did not walk in His ways.
But for me it is good that the Lord has humbled me, so that I may keep His commandments."
And he bore the oppressions of that wicked man with courage, for he remembered the word of God that says:
"Blessed are you when they persecute you and revile you, and falsely speak every evil word against you for my sake."
While the martyr of Christ was still imprisoned in Tbilisi, he wrote letters to all the hermits of the city and the superiors of the monastery, in which it was written:
"I know that you have heard what God has brought upon me because of my sins. But I entreat you, holy fathers
and true ascetics of Christ, to remember my love and my faith toward you, and to be willing to pray for me to the Lord,
not only that He may deliver me from the hands of the lawless one, but that Christ, the true God, may give me strength
against this snare set before me, which my enemy has laid, who wishes to make me stumble from the path my soul longs for."
After a few days they bound him with harsh iron fetters and sent him to the land of Babylon,
to the city called Samarra. They brought him to the king of the Ishmaelites, whose name was Jafar, son of Abraham.
When they brought the martyr of Christ before him, the king said to him: "Behold, you have been given into my hands, and I have power over you to do good or evil.
But listen to me and obey me: accept our law and renounce your error concerning Christ as God, for I see that you are a man of understanding.
How then can you confess as God a mere man, born of a woman?
Stop this from now on, for it cannot be said how God could have a Son.
But now turn away from your error, and receive from me good things and the highest honour, and I will make you my counsellor and more glorious than all your companions.
And if you do not listen to me, you will surely die by the edge of the sword, and I will give your flesh as food to the birds of the sky. And who is there who will deliver you from my hands?"
The holy martyr of Christ answered him and said: "I also know that you have power over my body, but not over my soul, as my Lord and God says.
Therefore I do not fear your sword. Instead I fear Him who is able to destroy both soul and body, and who also has the power to give life, just as He has the power to put to death.
Therefore I endure with joy for His name's sake, for He is the true God, the mighty Ruler and Prince of Peace, the Father of the ages to come," as it is written.
"So how could I despise Him and obey your command and your law, which the prophet rebukes, saying:
'It has not been heard of in Canaan, nor has it been seen in Teman, nor among the sons of Hagar, the kings and the storytellers, the seekers of understanding on the earth.
But they did not understand the way of truth, nor did they remember its paths, and they perished like it.'
Now, how should I listen to those whom the prophet accuses in this way and threatens with destruction? Do to me whatever you intend."
When the king heard these words, he was filled with great anger, and the wrath of his anger blazed against him even more fiercely.
And he ordered him to be put into a harsh prison.
And he sent to him the two princes who had also been brought as captives from Armenia and who had been honoured by him for denying Christ.
When they came, they said to the blessed man: "Our lord the king says this: 'I am rebuking your folly once more, because our law requires us to rebuke unbelievers three times.
Now listen to us so that you may live, and do not trust in that hopeless hope of yours, for God has given you into our hands.' And we too advise you the same.
Do not persist in that stubbornness of yours like a senseless man, for we know you to be wise. We too were Christians,
but we could not resist the king's command, and for this we gained honour from him. As for that eternal life, who knows what is better!"
Then the holy Constantine answered the envoys and said: "Tell your king:
'Do you really expect such a deed from me? Even if the custom of the kings of Babylon compels you,
for they too were opponents of the truth, give your command: whatever you intend to do, do it.'
And you, why do you keep standing over me and pressing me to become like you?
From now on, go away from me, so that I may search out [?] the commandments of my God."
And he raised his hands to heaven, opened his mouth in front of them, and said: "I sing praise to you, O Lord, God of hosts, God of the ages,
you who gave me strength to stand against this wicked judge, just as you said beforehand: "Give me your hearts, and I will give you my strength."
Make me worthy of the light of your face, for I have fled to you, O Christ, Son of God.
And see, I have been worn down by all the heathen for the sake of your holy name, and above all by this lawless king.
And now, O Lord my God, accept this sacrifice of mine, receive my soul out of the hands of the heathen, and grant me the promise that you promised, saying:
"Those who confess me before men, my Father will honour."
And just as in this very place you glorified those holy youths who confessed you, make me also worthy to be with them, you who appeared among them as the fourth.
And just as I confess you before this lawless king, you too, O good Lord, confess me before your angels.
And just as on this very day you glorified your worthy martyr, Saint George, and accepted his labours and the shedding of his spotless blood,
accept also this unworthy blood of mine, and give me a portion with him, so that my lot may fall with your chosen ones, for your inheritance is sure for me."
And while the holy martyr was saying this, streams of tears ran down from his eyes, as was his custom.
But those standing around him struck him on the face and tormented him with many torments, yet they could not stop his tongue from singing praise.
Then the commanders went back and told the king everything they had heard and seen.
Then the king grew even angrier. He sent them out and ordered them to cut off his head, but he was also testing them by this, because he was suspicious of them.
They went and struck at his neck with a sword in front of the dalich [?], but they could do him no harm at all.
When this was reported to the lawless king, he sent one of his attendants, a man of foreign race. That man cut off his head with a sword and brought it to his king,
just as the head of John the Baptist was brought to Herod. And they hung his body on a very high stake.
All the people saw a great sign over the body. And the holy martyr of Christ went to the place of rest,
from which all pains, sorrows, and afflictions have fled away, where the light of your face is seen, O Lord,
where the tongues of slanderers cannot reach, but there is endless joy there and fellowship with the holy angels.
He died in good confession on the tenth of the month of November, on the feast of Saint George, whose companion he became.
The day was Friday. The years from the creation were six thousand four hundred and fifty-seven, and by the reckoning of the Ishmaelites, two hundred and thirty-two.
Of the many brave deeds of Saint Constantine, this little has been written down, so that this account may be brief yet complete, and may not be tiresome through being incomplete
nor excessive through being drawn out, to the glory of the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, now and always and for ever and ever. Amen.
And when the holy kings mentioned earlier heard of the martyrdom of Saint Constantine,
They rejoiced with great joy and wrote a letter to his children and to the kinsfolk of his house, for they were very many. In it was written as follows:
"The words that first reached our ears told of what you were doing for righteousness' sake, and this was being proclaimed.
But now the deeds you have done are witnesses for you. What was said has been fully confirmed, and your piety has been well planted.
And truly this is the work of your zeal. On that small occasion, which confirmed the faith of your hearts, you made that faith manifest against the godless.
As perfect Christians, standing together, you became of one word. You were as if under one law, and at all times you saw the Lord face to face.

Unshaken, you stood by one another in the hope of Christ against the enemies of the Cross. With Christ you eagerly acted like men. You filled their faces with insult, and, united with those clothed in victory, you made their flight plain to see.
This was done by the power of God: a deed brought to completion and the boast of your fathers. And so that we may make our words sweet for ourselves and for you,
it is fitting to speak of this blessed martyr Constantine and of how bravely he stood against the invisible enemies.
"And I will show you, our beloved, who are truly his children and the images of his bodily life,

how, when he fought against the demons in the fear of God, he set his own flesh before them. He did not look to the richness of the affairs of bodily life. Nor did the light of this passing sun seem bright
to him, nor did the fading radiance of the sun's orb seem sweet to him. In his longing [lit. 'wrath'] for the light that is to come, he saw this rising sun as a cloud,
and out of love for Christ, all the tastes of the world, like blood from the teeth,
he spat out in this way, through the desire of that great longing and through the wisdom of his thought toward [?] (brotherhood?).
"For this reason he counted all the glory of this world as refuse, so that he might gain Christ alone.
And now, for this reason, the heavens and the earth and everything in them are his, for he left everything behind and boasted in God alone.
He is praised by God and by his angels, and he will be praised for his deeds for ever.
"Now we have no need to console you about him, since he is the consoler and intercessor for us and for you before Christ.

But let us now leave this subject, which cannot be left, and turn our word to you, who are accepted by God and are with us. By word and deed I make known to you the honour your position holds before us, for the sake of the honour of that departed one,
so that you may be confident toward me and be sheltered under the wings of my kingship. For you look to the will of the law, and everyone
who opposes it rejects Christ. Listen eagerly to Christ speaking among you, and humble yourselves before those anointed by him.
Stretch out your necks under our yoke, which comes from Christ, and do not cast off from your shoulders the carrying of our light burden.
You are true believers who trust in the Lord. You have become like Mount Zion, and you have shown yourselves to be a tower of strength before the face of the enemy. Make it plain by your deeds
that you have eagerly followed in the footsteps of your blessed father, who was a marvel to God and to men: by your love of strangers, by keeping the roads at peace,
and by taking in monks and people from far away. Now hold firm in this, and carry through to completion the way of life of that blessed man.
For the protection of our kingship will strive on your behalf, and the mountain of our greatness, which comes from Christ, will set right what has made you stumble.
So now act on this, and take courage from it.
"We command this not only to you but to all the Georgians who are on our side and under our hand.
For we count all who love Christ and belong to our God-given kingship as our own children, together with you. So rise up again and be strengthened by the Lord.
"And by the greatness of his might make your spears flash against your enemies, and do not give any of them a place to settle among you,
so that you may receive our favor, and receive from the Lord the honor promised to those who do good."
